title: Southwest Airlines Slashes 2026 Profit Forecast Amid Rising Fuel Costs, CNBC Reports
body:
Southwest Airlines announced on Monday that it is trimming its 2026 profit outlook, joining two of its domestic rivals in revising expectations after a sustained surge in jet fuel costs. The carrier, which has long marketed itself as a low‑fare, no‑frills alternative, said the higher price of fuel—its single largest operating expense—has forced a recalibration of earnings projections, even as demand for seats remains robust.

The revised guidance reflects a $150‑million reduction in the airline’s expected net income for the 2026 fiscal year, cutting the forecast to a range of $2.5 billion to $2.8 billion, down from the previously disclosed $2.65 billion to $3.0 billion. Southwest’s chief executive, Bob Jordan, emphasized that the airline continues to see strong booking trends, with passengers willing to absorb modest fare increases to secure seats on its extensive domestic network. “Travelers are still out there, still booking, and still choosing Southwest,” Jordan said in a conference call, adding that the company’s operational discipline and hedging program have helped mitigate some of the fuel price shock.

Southwest’s forecast adjustment follows similar moves by American Airlines and United Airlines, both of which have also lowered their 2026 earnings expectations in recent weeks. The three carriers collectively account for the majority of U.S. passenger traffic, and their outlooks are closely watched as barometers of the broader airline industry’s health. Analysts point to a confluence of factors that have tightened profit margins across the sector: volatile oil markets driven by geopolitical tensions, a lingering supply‑chain bottleneck that has kept refinery output below pre‑pandemic levels, and the Federal Reserve’s higher interest rates that have increased financing costs for aircraft acquisitions.

Despite the profit downgrade, Southwest’s balance sheet remains relatively strong. The airline reported a cash reserve of $7.2 billion at the end of the first quarter, providing a cushion to weather continued fuel volatility. Moreover, the carrier’s “fuel‑price hedging” strategy—locking in a portion of its fuel purchases at predetermined rates—has limited exposure to spot‑price spikes, though the hedges are set to expire in the latter half of 2025. When those contracts run out, Southwest may face additional pressure unless it can secure new hedges at favorable terms or pass further costs onto consumers.

Industry observers note that the airline’s ability to sustain demand despite higher fares underscores a broader shift in traveler behavior. After the pandemic, many passengers have placed a premium on flexibility, reliability and the perceived safety of larger carriers. Southwest’s “no‑change‑fees” policy and its extensive point‑to‑point route structure continue to attract both leisure and business travelers, especially on short‑haul routes where price sensitivity is lower. However, the airline’s all‑domestic focus leaves it more exposed to U.S. fuel price dynamics than carriers with a larger international footprint that can benefit from diversified fuel sourcing and varying tax regimes.

Looking ahead, the trajectory of Southwest’s profitability will hinge on several variables. If global oil markets stabilize and the company can lock in longer‑term hedges, the fuel cost impact could be softened, allowing the airline to reclaim some of the lost earnings margin. Conversely, any resurgence of geopolitical conflict or supply disruptions could keep fuel prices elevated, prompting further revisions to financial guidance. In the meantime, Southwest’s management remains confident that its operational efficiencies, disciplined cost structure, and resilient demand will enable it to navigate the headwinds and return to a growth path in the latter half of the decade.
